newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria finance min supports currency board plan.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria finance min supports currency board plan.

text.p: Bulgaria's Finance Minister Dimitar Kostov said on Monday the currency board proposed by the IMF would improve financial discipline paramount to economic recovery, but the final decision lay with parliament.

"The introduction of a currency board is more likely to succeed in achieving the level of financial discipline which Bulgaria needs now," Kostov told reporters after a meeting between IMF officials and Prime Minister Zhan Videnov.
"The final decision must come from parliament," he added.

An International Monetary Fund (IMF) team met Videnov as part of week-long talks with local politicians and bankers on introducing a currency board to stabilise the country's economy by curbing inflation and restoring confidence in the lev.

"A currency board would be a hopeful sign for Bulgaria...The only lasting solution to Bulgarian problems has to have a lasting and drastic reduction in inflation," Deputy Director of the IMF European Department, Michael Deppler, told journalists.

New IMF missions will come to discuss technical aspects of the implementation of a currency board in the next few weeks while the debate goes forward, said Deppler, who is due to leave Sofia on Tuesday.
Under the currency board system, the amount of national currency in circulation must be exactly matched by the central bank's hard currency reserves.
Currency boards, pegging the local currency usually to the dollar, have been used by Argentina, Estonia, Lithuania and Latvia to restore confidence and help defeat hyperinflation.

Bulgaria is caught in a vicious circle between lack of popular confidence in the lev and higher interest rates that the budget can not afford, Deppler said in an interview with Capital business weekly.

In terms of monetary arrangements, the alternatives to a currency board are floating exchange rates and a fixed exchange rate, both of which usually entail higher interest rates and are no longer applicable to Bulgaria, which has a floating rate now.
Deppler told Capital that the Fund's reform programme in Bulgaria had failed so far.
Bulgaria has overshot all of its budget targets for this year and has postponed drafting the 1997 budget until the end of December due to unpredictability of the interest rate, currently 180 percent.
If Bulgaria accepts the currency board plan, it would be best to draft the 1997 budget focusing on the requirements of the currency board, Deppler told Capital.

The IMF has twice postponed a $115 million loan due to Bulgaria's failure to meet reform targets which include curbing inflation, stabilising the exchange rate, speeding up privatisation and closing loss-making enterprises.
"Bulgarians need to make a new start and need a firm financial foundation for this new start," Deppler said after the meeting with Videnov.
